title: How to automate a website that has no API | 50agents
description: Automate a website with no API: try exports, email alerts and integrations first, then a browser tool that signs in once and asks before it submits.
h1: How to automate a website that has no API
answer: First look for a back door: an existing integration, an email the site already sends, or an export.
If there is none, use a recorder or a browser agent that keeps you signed in and asks before it submits anything.

chooser.h2: Which way in does your site offer?

root.q: Is the site in an automation catalog?

then.why: Even if the site's own docs mention no API, a catalog entry means someone built the connection. Search viaSocket's catalog of 2,300+ apps by the site's name.

then.q: Does it email you, or let you export?

then.answer: Automate from the email or the export
then.why: A supplier emails each invoice; an automation reads that email instead of the portal. Far steadier than clicking.

then.q: Does the page layout change often?

options.label: No, it is a stable tool

then.why: Record the clicks once and replay them; Chrome's Recorder can edit each step. Same result every run, until the site changes.

options.label: Yes, or I mostly read it

then.why: It reads the page and looks for what you described, so small layout changes rarely break it. It needs approvals for anything it submits.

head: Recorder or script
Browser agent
rows: Stable tools, many runs a day

body.p: Either way, the site's rules apply. Check its terms, keep to what a person would do by hand, and stop at CAPTCHAs: they are the site saying no.

method.h2: How to automate a website with no API

steps.title: Write the job as a person does it
steps.body: "Sign in, open Reports, choose last month, download the CSV." Every step, every click. If you cannot write it, a tool cannot do it.

steps.title: Split reading from doing
steps.body: Reading a page is low risk. Submitting a form, placing an order or changing a setting is not. Plan for every "doing" step to ask you first.

steps.title: Sort out the sign-in
steps.body: Sign in yourself once in the tool's browser and let it keep the session. Expect to sign in again when the site logs you out.

note.text: Never paste a password into a chat or a shared sheet. A tool that needs your password typed in for it is the wrong tool.

steps.title: Run it once while you watch
steps.body: Most tools show the browser live or record what it did. Watch the first run end to end.

steps.title: Add a check that it worked
steps.body: A file downloaded, a confirmation number on the page, a row count. Without a check, a failed run looks like a quiet one.

steps.title: Schedule it no more than needed
steps.body: Daily or weekly is enough for most portals, and keeps you well inside what the site expects from a person.

captain.line: Captain sets up a browser agent with a browser of its own. When the portal wants a sign-in, it asks you to sign in there yourself, then carries on.
captain.ask: Set up a browser agent that reads last week's invoices on my supplier portal every Monday and tells me the total

wrong.title: The site changed and the script broke
wrong.body: Recorded clicks point at a button that moved. Keep scripts short, and prefer a browser agent for pages that change often.

wrong.title: Signed out mid-run
wrong.body: Sessions expire and two-step sign-in comes back. Expect a sign-in request every few weeks.

wrong.title: A submit went through twice
wrong.body: A retry repeated the last step. Have every submit ask first, and check for the confirmation before trying again.

wrong.title: Blocked by the site
wrong.body: Too many visits, or the site does not want automation. Slow down; if it shows a CAPTCHA, stop.

faqs.q: Can I automate a website without an API?
faqs.a: Yes, by driving a browser: a recorder replays clicks, a browser agent reads the page and decides where to click. Check first for an export, an email notification or an existing integration, which are more reliable.

faqs.q: Is this the same as RPA?
faqs.a: Close. RPA (robotic process automation) is the older name for software that clicks through screens like a person. Browser agents add AI to read pages that change.

faqs.q: Will it break when the site changes?
faqs.a: Recorded scripts often do. Browser agents cope with small changes and can still misread a redesigned page, so keep a check at the end of each run.

faqs.q: Is it allowed to automate a website?
faqs.a: Check the site's terms first. Keep to what a person would do by hand, at a pace a person would, and stop at CAPTCHAs: a CAPTCHA is the site saying no.

faqs.q: Can it download files for me?
faqs.a: Yes. "Sign in, open Reports, choose last month, download the CSV" is a typical job. Make the downloaded file the run's check, so a failed run never looks like a quiet one.
Daily or weekly is enough for most portals. It keeps the job well inside what the site expects from a person, and fewer runs mean fewer sign-ins to fix.
